questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Density-independent regulation
questions.stem: Historical case 1 asks which factor regulates a population regardless of its density.

options.text: A drought that kills a fixed proportion
Predation that rises with prey density

questions.explanation: Density-independent factors such as weather affect a fixed proportion regardless of population size. Competition, predation and disease usually depend on density.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Density-dependent regulation
questions.stem: Historical case 2 asks which factor becomes stronger as population density rises.
questions.explanation: Density-dependent factors such as competition intensify as density increases. Weather and disasters are largely density-independent.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Delayed density dependence
questions.stem: Historical case 3 asks why a population can overshoot carrying capacity before declining.
questions.explanation: When regulation responds with a time lag, the population can exceed carrying capacity before the feedback reduces it.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Assumptions behind an exponential model
questions.learningObjective: State an assumption of exponential growth
questions.stem: Historical case 4 asks which assumption underlies exponential growth.
questions.explanation: Exponential growth assumes unlimited resources and a constant per-capita growth rate. Carrying capacity and density dependence belong to logistic growth.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Per-capita rate of increase from births and deaths
questions.stem: Historical case 5 gives 120 births and 40 deaths in a population of 1000 in one year; what is r?
questions.explanation: Per-capita rate of increase is births minus deaths divided by population, so (120 minus 40) divided by 1000 equals 0.08 per year.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Growth rate from two counts five years apart
questions.learningObjective: Compute growth rate from two counts
questions.stem: Historical case 6 counts 100 individuals in 2010 and 160 in 2015; what is the annual growth rate r?
questions.explanation: Using Nt = N0 e^rt, r equals ln(160/100) divided by 5, which is about 0.098 per year. The count interval is five years.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The finite rate of increase
questions.stem: Historical case 7 gives r equals 0.1 per year; what is lambda?
questions.explanation: Lambda equals e raised to r, so e to the 0.1 is about 1.105. Lambda is the finite rate of increase per time step.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Logistic rate of increase at a stated size
questions.learningObjective: Compute logistic growth rate at a given size
questions.stem: Historical case 8 has r equals 0.5, K equals 1000 and N equals 500; what is dN/dt?
questions.explanation: Logistic growth is rN(1 minus N/K), so 0.5 times 500 times (1 minus 500/1000) equals 125 individuals per time unit.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Maximum sustainable yield on a logistic curve
questions.learningObjective: Find MSY on a logistic curve
questions.stem: Historical case 9 asks where maximum sustainable yield occurs on a logistic curve.

options.misconception: harvest at K is zero growth

options.text: At one quarter of carrying capacity

questions.explanation: On a logistic curve, growth rate is maximal at K/2, so maximum sustainable yield occurs there. At K growth is zero.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Overshoot and collapse
questions.stem: Historical case 10 asks what overshoot and collapse means.
questions.explanation: Overshoot occurs when a population exceeds carrying capacity, followed by a crash as resources are depleted.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Life expectancy from a cohort life table
questions.learningObjective: Compute life expectancy from a table
questions.stem: Historical case 11 gives 1000 individuals at birth and total person-years 5000; what is e0?
questions.explanation: Life expectancy at birth is total person-years divided by the cohort size, so 5000 divided by 1000 equals 5 years. The inputs are simplified.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Mortality between two ages in a life table
questions.stem: Historical case 12 has 800 alive at age 5 and 720 at age 6; what is the mortality rate between these ages?
questions.explanation: Mortality between ages is deaths divided by those alive at the start, so (800 minus 720) divided by 800 equals 0.1.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Net reproductive rate from a life table
questions.stem: Historical case 13 gives survivorship 0.5 at age 2 and fecundity 4 at that age; what is R0 if only that age reproduces?
questions.explanation: R0 is the sum of survivorship times fecundity, so 0.5 times 4 equals 2. An R0 above one means population growth.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Generation time from a life table
questions.stem: Historical case 14 gives R0 equals 2 and the weighted age sum equals 6; what is generation time T?
questions.explanation: Generation time is the weighted sum of ages divided by R0, so 6 divided by 2 equals 3 years. It is the mean age of mothers.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Approximate growth rate from R0 and T
questions.learningObjective: Approximate r from R0 and T
questions.stem: Historical case 15 gives R0 equals 2 and T equals 5 years; what is the approximate r?
questions.explanation: The approximation r is ln(R0) divided by T, so ln(2) divided by 5 is about 0.139 per year. It assumes stable age distribution.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Growth rate solved from the renewal equation
questions.stem: Historical case 16 solves the renewal equation and finds r equals 0.2; what does this imply?
questions.explanation: The renewal equation gives the exact growth rate satisfying the life table. A value of 0.2 means the population grows by about 20 percent per year.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why the two growth-rate estimates differ
questions.learningObjective: Explain difference between approximate and exact r
questions.stem: Historical case 17 asks why the approximate r from R0 and T differs from the renewal solution.

options.text: Because the approximation ignores age structure
Because the renewal equation is exact only for bacteria

questions.explanation: The approximation ln(R0)/T assumes stable age distribution and ignores detailed age structure, while the renewal equation uses the full life table.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Reading a survivorship curve from a cohort
questions.stem: Historical case 18 shows a curve with high early survival and a steep drop in old age; which type is this?
questions.explanation: Type I curves show high survival early and mortality concentrated in old age, typical of large mammals. Type III has high early mortality.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Steps in building a life table
questions.stem: Historical case 19 asks which step comes first when building a life table.
questions.explanation: A life table begins by following a cohort and recording survival by age. Fecundity, R0 and generation time are derived later.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Fecundity against longevity as a trade-off
questions.stem: Historical case 20 asks why high fecundity often reduces longevity.

options.text: Because energy spent on reproduction reduces survival

questions.explanation: Energy allocated to reproduction cannot be used for maintenance and survival, creating a trade-off between fecundity and longevity.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Mark and recapture population estimate
questions.stem: Historical case 21 marks 50 animals, later captures 80, of which 20 are marked; what is the population estimate?
questions.explanation: The Lincoln-Petersen estimate is marked in first sample times total second sample divided by marked in second sample, so 50 times 80 divided by 20 equals 200.
questions.hint: Use M times C divided by R

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a recapture estimate falls low
questions.stem: Historical case 22 asks why a mark-recapture estimate can be too low.

options.text: Because marks are lost or marked animals die

questions.explanation: If marked animals are more likely to be recaptured, the recapture count is high, which lowers the population estimate. Trap-happiness creates downward bias.
questions.hint: Are marked animals easier to catch?

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Population size from successive removals
questions.stem: Historical case 23 removes 30, then 20, then 10 animals in successive samples; estimate initial population using the removal method simplification?
questions.explanation: A simple removal estimate treats the declining catches as a geometric decline; here the three catches sum to 60 and the pattern suggests about 100 initially. The value is an illustrative estimate.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Assumptions the removal method needs
questions.learningObjective: State an assumption of the removal method
questions.stem: Historical case 24 asks which assumption the removal method requires.
questions.explanation: The removal method assumes constant catchability so that declining catches reflect declining population. Changing catchability invalidates the estimate.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Population total from a fixed-area census
questions.stem: Historical case 25 counts 40 individuals in a 2 hectare plot; what is density per hectare?
questions.explanation: Density is count divided by area, so 40 divided by 2 equals 20 individuals per hectare. The plot is assumed representative.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Condition factor from weight and length
questions.stem: Historical case 26 has weight 100 g and length 10 cm; using K equals 100 times W over L cubed, what is K?
questions.explanation: K equals 100 times 100 divided by 10 cubed, which is 10000 divided by 1000, or 10. The factor scales weight by length cubed.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Length at age from a growth relation
questions.stem: Historical case 27 uses L equals L infinity times (1 minus e to the minus k t) with L infinity 100, k 0.2, t 5; what is L?
questions.explanation: L equals 100 times (1 minus e to the minus 1), which is about 100 times 0.632, or 63.2 cm. The parameters describe asymptotic growth.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Growth in length against growth in weight
questions.learningObjective: Relate length growth to weight growth
questions.stem: Historical case 28 asks how weight changes when length doubles under isometric growth.
questions.explanation: Under isometric growth, weight scales with volume, which scales with length cubed. Doubling length gives 2 cubed, or 8 times the weight.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Cohort survival under a constant annual mortality
questions.stem: Historical case 29 starts with 1000 individuals and 20 percent annual mortality; how many survive after one year?
questions.explanation: Survivors equal 1000 times (1 minus 0.2), which is 800. The mortality is applied once for one year.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The Allee effect
questions.stem: Historical case 30 asks what the Allee effect describes.

options.text: Per-capita growth declines at low density
Growth rate increases as density decreases

questions.explanation: The Allee effect is reduced per-capita growth at low density, often due to difficulty finding mates or cooperating. It can create a minimum viable population.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Per-capita growth below an Allee threshold
questions.learningObjective: Predict growth below an Allee threshold
questions.stem: Historical case 31 places a population below its Allee threshold; what is likely?
questions.explanation: Below the Allee threshold, per-capita growth is negative, so the population declines toward extinction unless rescued.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Time for an invading population to grow a hundredfold
questions.stem: Historical case 32 has r equals 0.1 per year; how many years to grow a hundredfold?
questions.explanation: Time equals ln(100) divided by r, so 4.605 divided by 0.1 equals 46.05 years. The calculation assumes exponential growth.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Assumptions hidden in the logistic model
questions.stem: Historical case 33 asks which assumption is hidden in the logistic model.

options.text: Growth rate is independent of density

questions.explanation: The logistic model assumes a fixed carrying capacity and no time lags or age structure. Real systems often violate these.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Eradication declared on the last sighting
questions.stem: Historical case 34 declares eradication after the last sighting; is this justified?

options.text: Yes, absence of sightings proves absence
Yes, if the species is rare
No, because all species are immortal

questions.explanation: Absence of sightings does not prove absence. Undetected individuals can remain, so eradication claims need thorough surveys.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Threshold for herd immunity
questions.stem: Historical case 35 has R0 equals 4; what proportion must be immune for herd immunity?
questions.explanation: Herd immunity threshold is 1 minus 1/R0, so 1 minus 1/4 equals 0.75. At least 75 percent must be immune.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Density-dependent transmission
questions.stem: Historical case 36 asks which transmission increases with host density.
questions.explanation: Direct contact transmission rises with host density because more contacts occur. Other modes may be frequency-dependent or independent.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Square-root dependence on two host densities
questions.stem: Historical case 37 has host densities 100 and 400; if transmission scales with the square root of their product, what is the factor?
questions.explanation: The factor is the square root of 100 times 400, which is the square root of 40000, or 200. This is a simplified transmission kernel.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Breeding sites as a control point
questions.learningObjective: Identify a control point in population regulation
questions.stem: Historical case 38 asks why removing breeding sites can control a population.

options.text: Because it limits a key resource

questions.explanation: Breeding sites are a limiting resource; removing them reduces reproduction and population growth. It does not increase fecundity or carrying capacity.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Economic threshold for pest control
questions.stem: Historical case 39 asks what an economic threshold means in pest management.

options.text: The pest density where control costs equal damage costs
The density where pests go extinct
The density where no damage occurs
The density where pests are first detected

questions.explanation: The economic threshold is the pest density at which the cost of control equals the cost of damage. Below it, control is not cost-effective.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Break-even density for a pest treatment
questions.stem: Historical case 40 has damage cost 5 dollars per pest and control cost 100 dollars; what is the break-even pest density?
questions.explanation: Break-even occurs when damage cost times density equals control cost, so density equals 100 divided by 5, or 20 pests. Above this density, control pays.
questions.hint: Divide control cost by damage per pest

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Density-independent regulation
questions.stem: Historical case 41 asks which event is density-independent for a deer population.

options.text: Wolf predation rising with deer numbers
A severe winter killing a fixed proportion

questions.explanation: A severe winter kills a similar proportion regardless of density, making it density-independent. Predation, competition and disease depend on density.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Density-dependent regulation
questions.stem: Historical case 42 asks which factor is density-dependent for a plant population.
questions.explanation: Shading intensifies as plants grow and density increases, making it density-dependent. Frost, landslides and drought are largely density-independent.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Delayed density dependence
questions.stem: Historical case 43 asks which situation shows delayed density dependence.

options.text: Constant birth rate at all densities
Predator population peaks one year after prey

questions.explanation: A predator peak lagging behind prey density is a classic delayed density-dependent response. Instant effects show no lag.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Assumptions behind an exponential model
questions.stem: Historical case 44 asks which condition violates exponential growth assumptions.
questions.explanation: Exponential growth assumes no carrying capacity. Introducing a carrying capacity of 500 switches the model to logistic growth.

questions.explanation: Per-capita growth rate is birth rate minus death rate, so 0.3 minus 0.1 equals 0.2 per year.

questions.explanation: Using Nt = N0 e^rt, r equals ln(320/200) divided by 5, which is about 0.098 per year. The interval is five years.

questions.explanation: Logistic growth is rN(1 minus N/K), so 0.4 times 250 times (1 minus 250/500) equals 50 individuals per time unit.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Maximum sustainable yield on a logistic curve
questions.stem: Historical case 49 has r equals 0.4 and K equals 1000; what is the maximum sustainable yield?
questions.explanation: MSY equals rK/4, so 0.4 times 1000 divided by 4 equals 100. This is the maximum harvest at K/2.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Overshoot and collapse
questions.stem: Historical case 50 asks what follows a population overshooting carrying capacity.

options.text: A decline as resources are depleted
Immediate stabilisation at the higher level

questions.explanation: Overshoot depletes resources, leading to a decline or crash. The population cannot stay above carrying capacity indefinitely.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Life expectancy from a cohort life table
questions.stem: Historical case 51 asks what life expectancy at birth represents.

options.text: The age at which all individuals die
The survival rate at age zero
The number of births per female
The average years lived by a cohort

questions.explanation: Life expectancy at birth is the average number of years lived by individuals in a cohort. It is not the maximum age or fecundity.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Mortality between two ages in a life table
questions.stem: Historical case 52 asks what a mortality rate between ages measures.

options.text: The proportion dying in that interval

questions.explanation: The mortality rate between ages is the proportion of those alive at the start who die during the interval. It is not population size or births.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Net reproductive rate from a life table
questions.stem: Historical case 53 asks what R0 greater than 1 implies.
questions.explanation: R0 is the average number of female offspring per female. Above 1, the population grows; below 1, it declines; at 1, it is stable.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Generation time from a life table
questions.stem: Historical case 54 asks what generation time represents.

options.text: The time to reach carrying capacity
The mean age of mothers at childbirth

questions.explanation: Generation time is the average age at which females give birth, weighted by their reproductive output. It is not lifespan or census interval.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science

questions.topic: Approximate growth rate from R0 and T
questions.stem: Historical case 55 asks when the approximation r equals ln(R0)/T is most useful.

options.text: When detailed age data are unavailable
When exact renewal solutions are required

questions.explanation: The approximation is useful when only R0 and generation time are known, without full age-specific data. It is not exact.

options.text: An approximate r from R0 only
An exact r from the full life table

questions.explanation: The renewal equation uses age-specific survivorship and fecundity to solve for the exact intrinsic growth rate r.

questions.stem: Historical case 57 asks why approximate and exact r can differ in magnitude.

options.text: Because the approximation smooths age structure

questions.explanation: The approximation collapses age structure into R0 and T, so it can differ from the exact renewal solution when age structure matters.

questions.topic: Reading a survivorship curve from a cohort
questions.stem: Historical case 58 shows high early mortality and flat survival later; which type is this?
questions.explanation: Type III curves have high mortality early in life, with survivors living to older ages. Many invertebrates and plants show this pattern.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Steps in building a life table
questions.stem: Historical case 59 asks which quantity is derived last in a life table.
questions.explanation: Generation time depends on R0 and the weighted age sum, so it is derived after survivorship, fecundity and R0. It is among the last quantities calculated.

questions.topic: Fecundity against longevity as a trade-off
questions.stem: Historical case 60 asks why a species with many offspring often has short lifespan.

options.text: Because energy for reproduction reduces survival

questions.explanation: Energy allocated to producing many offspring reduces energy available for maintenance and survival, shortening lifespan.
